quote: Please move this function call to `abortFetch`.
why: cleanupAbortListeners() is called ad hoc at each exit point (direct abort, network-error reject, end-of-body) instead of once inside abortFetch/shared teardown; it's easy for a future exit path to forget the call and re-leak the abort listener the PR is trying to fix.

quote: There might be some unexpected behavior when cloning the response, so we need to investigate.
why: Wrapping processResponseEndOfBody in a new closure that also runs cleanupAbortListeners changes when/how the response is handled relative to response cloning; reviewer flags this as an unverified behavior change rather than a pure refactor, i.e. a potential regression risk in an untested path.

quote: At this point, if stored correctly, the key matcher does not need new normalization, isn't it?
why: normalizeOrigin is called again on keyMatcher inside the matching loop even though matchers are expected to already be normalized when stored, causing redundant recomputation on every dispatch/lookup.

quote: On L59 the origin is already normalized by the caller, we can save another normalization, wdyt?
why: dispatch() normalizes opts.origin and passes it into this.get(), but get() (and the code path here) normalizes it again, doing the same URL parsing/lowercasing work twice for a single request.

quote: Same as per the getter one, unless this is called explicitly somewhere else and the origin is not normalized, we can save this call as well
why: kMockAgentSet re-normalizes an origin that, per the caller's own contract, should already be normalized by the time it reaches this method, adding an unnecessary extra normalization call on the hot path.

quote: The `URL` already does the parsing into lower case as part of the spec
why: The new normalizeOrigin implementation manually lowercases url.hostname, but the WHATWG URL spec already normalizes hostnames to lowercase, so the extra .toLowerCase() step is based on a false premise about what URL does and is redundant/misleading code.

quote: this should never happen, why is there this guard?
why: The isActiveStream() early-return in the 'response' handler defends against a request no longer belonging to its HTTP/2 stream; flagging it as unexplained surfaces that the request-to-stream association can change under GOAWAY handling without the invariant being documented or the listeners being detached, which is exactly the kind of unclear bookkeeping that causes stale-callback bugs.

The same unexplained isActiveStream() guard is duplicated in the 'end' handler; the reviewer flags that the pattern is copy-pasted per event handler instead of centrally preventing stale requests from receiving stream events at all.

quote: Following @mcollina point, maybe we can fully detach the `stream` events at this points; maybe keep a reference of the `stream` itself to the `request` to cleanup upon gracefull shutdown
why: On GOAWAY, requests are unlinked from their stream (kRequestStreamId set to null) but the stream's event listeners referencing the request are never removed, so the request object and its closures stay reachable/alive via those listeners instead of being cleaned up, and the pattern relies on ad hoc isActiveStream() checks in every handler rather than actual detachment.

quote: I don't see this being imported anywhere
why: defaultMaxEventSize is added to module.exports but no other module imports it, meaning the new EventSource event-size limit configuration this export exists to support is not actually wired up anywhere, i.e. dead/unused code masking a missing integration.

getEventDataSize() branches on `event === this.event`, but the reviewer notes the stream can only ever be processing one event at a time, so the false branch is unreachable dead code that hides what the function is actually supposed to do (or signals a wrong assumption about when it can be called with a stale event).

quote: same here, we can only ever have 1 event at a time
why: setEventDataSize() repeats the same always-true `event === this.event` guard as getEventDataSize(), so the size bookkeeping silently no-ops whenever the premise doesn't hold instead of asserting or erroring, which would hide the event-size limit failing to track the current event correctly.

quote: new URL(originString).origin always removes the trailing slash, so normalizeOrigin('http://example.com/', false) becomes 'http://example.com'.
why: URL.origin never includes a path, so it never has a trailing slash to begin with regardless of input; the ignoreTrailingSlash branch a few lines below (checking originString.endsWith('/')) is therefore dead code that can never fire, silently making the option a no-op and causing slash-distinct mock origins to collide.

Only nullish values fall back to the default; a negative number or NaN passed as maxEventSize is accepted as-is. Because the enforcement check later is `this.maxEventSize > 0`, any negative or NaN value silently disables the limit exactly like the documented 0 sentinel, instead of being rejected as invalid configuration.

This is the only place maxEventSize is enforced, and it only runs from parseLine(), which _transform only calls once a full line (LF/CR) has been found. A data: line sent without a terminating newline is pushed into this.chunks indefinitely across chunks with no size check applied, so an unterminated line can grow unbounded in memory before the limit is ever checked.

The diff removes the prior client.emit('connectionError', client[kUrl], [client], err) call from onHttp2SessionGoAway without replacing it; every GOAWAY (including a genuine non-zero error code, not just the informational NGHTTP2_NO_ERROR case) now only ever emits 'disconnect'. Any consumer listening for 'connectionError' to distinguish a real failure from an ordinary shutdown silently stops being notified.
